intro: Skateboarding began on sidewalks and in empty pools, on ground that was never meant for it. As it grew, it ran into a hard question that every city must answer: who gets to use shared space? Some cities answered with metal knobs on ledges and signs that banned boards. Skaters answered with petitions, council meetings and, sometimes, bags of concrete poured under a bridge.

This unit follows two paths. The first stays close to home: the Southbank undercroft in London, saved by a campaign in 2014; Burnside in Portland, Oregon, built by skaters starting in 1990; and the Tony Hawk Foundation, now The Skatepark Project, which helps towns build public parks. The second goes around the world: Skateistan, which used skating to bring children in Kabul to school, and the Tokyo 2020 and Paris 2024 Olympic Games, where teenagers from Japan, Brazil, Australia and Great Britain won medals.

By the end you will be able to explain hostile design and the arguments for and against skateparks, describe how skaters have won space through civic action, name key Olympic medalists and events, and use simple physics to explain why a stopper throws a rider and how air time grows with height. You will also be able to take a side in skating's own debate about the Olympics and support it with facts.
bigQuestion: How have skaters claimed a place in cities and on the world stage, and what did they gain and give up along the way?

timeline.t: First National Skateboard Championships in Anaheim, California
Skaters begin riding the Southbank undercroft in London
Skaters begin building Burnside under a bridge in Portland, Oregon
ESPN holds the Extreme Games in Rhode Island, later the X Games
Tony Hawk starts the Tony Hawk Foundation to help build public skateparks
Oliver Percovich founds Skateistan in Kabul, Afghanistan
Long Live Southbank wins an agreement to keep the undercroft
The IOC adds skateboarding to the Olympic program
The Tony Hawk Foundation becomes The Skatepark Project
First Olympic skateboarding events at the Tokyo 2020 Games
Skateboarding at the Paris Games, at the Place de la Concorde

words.d: a knob, bracket or bump fixed to a ledge, rail or bench so a skateboard cannot grind or slide along it
shaping a public object so that certain people cannot use it in certain ways; also called defensive architecture
a place anyone may enter and use, such as a sidewalk, park or plaza
the tendency of an object to keep moving, or keep still, unless a force changes its motion
a number, written μ, that describes how strongly two surfaces resist sliding over each other
a covered space beneath a building; at Southbank, the skated space under the arts center
do-it-yourself; in skating, a spot that skaters build themselves
legal responsibility for harm, such as an injury on someone's property
an organization that uses the money it raises for its mission instead of paying it to owners
the world body that writes the rules for one sport and runs its qualifying events
in skating, how high a skater flies above the coping
a group with its own values, style and customs inside a larger society

test.q: Metal knobs bolted along a granite ledge are an example of what?
choices: a skate plaza feature made for grinding
a skate stopper, part of hostile design
test.why: Skate stoppers block grinding and are one kind of hostile design.

test.q: Which example of hostile design is aimed at people resting, not skaters?
choices: armrests spaced so no one can lie on a bench
test.why: Armrests that stop lying down are a common example of hostile design.

test.q: A skater moving at 3 m/s hits a stopper. Why is that dangerous?
choices: The board stops, but the body keeps moving forward by inertia.
The stopper speeds the board up suddenly.
Gravity stops working during a grind.
The wax on the ledge catches fire.
test.why: Inertia keeps the rider moving after the board is stopped.

choices: Wax raises the coefficient of friction, so boards grip.
Wax lowers the coefficient of friction, so slides go farther.
Wax protects the stone from all damage.
Wax is required by skatepark rules.
test.why: A lower μ gives a longer slide distance, v²/(2μg).

test.q: What makes the Southbank undercroft important in skate history?
choices: It was the first skatepark built by a city.
It hosted the first Olympic skateboarding event.
It has been skated since the 1970s and was saved by a 2014 campaign.
It is a drained swimming pool in California.
test.why: Skaters have used it since the 1970s, and Long Live Southbank kept it in 2014.

test.q: Which statement about Burnside is true?
choices: The city of London built it in 2014.
It is the Olympic park course.
Skaters built it under a bridge in Portland starting in 1990, and the city later accepted it.
test.why: Burnside began as an unpermitted, skater-built park in 1990.

choices: the Tony Hawk Foundation's name since 2020, helping build public parks
a campaign to save the Southbank undercroft
the federation that runs Olympic skating
test.why: Founded in 2002 as the Tony Hawk Foundation, it was renamed in 2020.

test.q: Which concern do opponents of skateparks often raise?
choices: too few skaters live in cities
noise, cost and liability for injuries
test.why: Neighbors and officials often worry about noise, cost and liability.

test.q: Who founded Skateistan, and in what year?
test.why: Oliver Percovich founded Skateistan in Kabul in 2007.

test.q: What are the two kinds of Olympic skateboarding events?
test.why: The Olympics hold street and park events for men and women.

test.q: Which medalists were thirteen years old at Tokyo 2020?
choices: Momiji Nishiya, Rayssa Leal and Sky Brown
test.why: Nishiya (gold) and Leal (silver) in street and Brown (bronze) in park were all thirteen.

test.q: Who won women's street gold at Paris 2024?
test.why: Coco Yoshizawa won women's street gold in Paris.

test.q: With g = 9.8 m/s², a 1.0 m air lasts about 0.90 s. About how long does a 2.0 m air last?
test.why: Air time grows with the square root of height: 2√(2 × 2.0 ÷ 9.8) ≈ 1.28 s, not double.

test.q: Why did some skaters oppose the Olympics?
choices: They thought skating had never had contests before.
They wanted the Games held only in California.
They believed helmets would be banned.
They feared teams, uniforms and judging would change skating's creative culture.
test.why: Critics saw skating as closer to art and worried about outside control.

test.q: Which shows that skating contests are older than the Olympics?
choices: The first National Skateboard Championships were held in Anaheim in 1965.
test.why: Contests date back to Anaheim in 1965, over fifty years before Tokyo.

write.prompt: Your town is deciding whether to build a public skatepark or add skate stoppers downtown. Write a letter to the council taking one side. Use at least two dates, people or places from this unit, answer one concern from the other side, and explain one physics idea that supports your view.
tips: Name a real case, such as Southbank in 2014 or Burnside in 1990.
Answer a concern such as noise, cost or liability directly.
Use inertia or friction to explain a safety point.
Keep each paragraph to one main reason.
End by saying exactly what you want the council to do.
